sentences.text: Crocodylus lucivenator is distinguished by a rostral boss, an expanded skull structure that runs along the dorsal surface just before the eyes.
The second posterior knob on the maxilla is more pronounced than the midrostral boss, adding to the distinctive cranial ornamentation.
Its skull table is trapezoidal and formed mainly by the frontal, parietal, postorbital, and squamosal bones.
Pronounced squamosal horns, produced by the postorbital bones, are most developed in the largest individuals.
The fourth premaxillary teeth and the fifth and tenth maxillary teeth are the largest in the upper jaw, fitting into a classic interlocking pattern.
Isolated osteoderms attributed to this species vary in shape, with some circular or D-shaped elements likely forming part of a nuchal shield or flank armor.
The largest specimens reached lengths of 4 to 5 meters and weighed between 300 and 600 kilograms, making them among the biggest crocodiles of the Pliocene.
A specimen of Crocodylus lucivenator preserves five furrows and a puncture wound on its lower jaw, with healed bone indicating the animal survived the injury for a considerable time.
The species name lucivenator combines Latin words for “light” and “hunter,” reflecting its presumed role as a prominent predator.
Crocodylus lucivenator was formally named in 2026 by Brochu and colleagues, who also described the species in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology.
The holotype, specimen A.L. 138-16, consists of a complete cranium with a matching lower jaw and originates from the SH-1 submember of the Sidi Hakoma Member.
The type locality is the Hadar Formation in Ethiopia, a site also known from the study titled “Lucy’s peril.”
Crocodylus lucivenator functioned as a large generalist ambush predator, likely occupying the apex position in its ecosystem.
Injuries on a specimen suggest it engaged in aggressive feeding behaviors such as the death roll or head thrashing, typical of crocodilian predation.
The puncture wound and associated furrows were caused by another crocodile rather than a mammal, indicating intraspecific conflict was a primary threat.
Healed bone texture shows the animal survived the injury, implying a capacity for recovery after severe trauma.
Crocodylus lucivenator belongs to the genus Crocodylus, which was named by Laurenti in 1768.
Its specific epithet is lucivenator, and it is placed within the Palaeoafrican Crocodylus clade, a group distinct from modern Neoafrican species such as the Nile and Sacred crocodiles.
Phylogenetic analysis positions it basally within the genus, branching off before the Indopacific clade and the split between Neoafrican and Neotropic taxa.
It appears more closely related to other Paleoafrican Crocodylus species from East Africa than to modern African crocodiles.
Crocodylus lucivenator lived during the Late Pliocene epoch in the Hadar Formation of Ethiopia.
The Hadar Formation comprised mixed woodlands and grasslands, with large paleolakes present at certain intervals.
Fossils of the species are found in three of the four members of the formation—Sidi Hakoma, Denen Dora, and Kada Hadar—reflecting its persistence across changing environments.
The oldest member of the formation was wetter and more wooded, while younger members record increasingly drier conditions.
The genus Crocodylus as a whole spans from the Campanian to the Holocene, a range of 83.6 to 0 million years ago.

There is ongoing debate about whether the Palaeoafrican group that includes Crocodylus lucivenator should be grouped with modern Neotropic Crocodylus, as alternative phylogenetic results are possible.
